title: The Papacy in the Dark Ages
orientation: This chapter opens Part II ('The Schoolmen') by tracing the papacy's turbulent fortunes from Gregory the Great to Sylvester II (roughly A.D. 600-1000), the period Russell calls the Dark Ages. It matters for the history of philosophy not because it contains philosophical argument -- it contains almost none -- but because it explains the political and institutional scaffolding (the papacy's independence from Byzantium, its alliance with the Franks, the Holy Roman Empire, the forged Donation of Constantine) within which medieval philosophy would later be produced and controlled.
historical_background: After Gregory the Great, the papacy oscillated between subjection to the Greek Emperor, the Western Emperor, and the local Roman aristocracy. Lombard pressure on Byzantine Italy pushed the popes into alliance with the Franks: Pepin's donation of Ravenna and the former Exarchate (754) created the Papal States and a permanent political break from Constantinople, later ratified in myth by the forged Donation of Constantine. Charlemagne's coronation as Emperor in Rome on Christmas Day, 800, revived the Western Empire and created a lasting, mutually galling interdependence between Pope and Emperor. Carolingian power decayed rapidly after Charlemagne; Pope Nicholas I briefly raised the papacy to new heights (858-867), but the tenth century saw it fall completely under the control of the Roman aristocracy (the Theophylact-Marozia family), coinciding with raids by Saracens, Magyars, and Normans. Russell treats the year 1000 as the low point of Western civilization, after which monastic reform and the cessation of invasions began a recovery that continued (in his view) until 1914.
philosophical_problems: What made it possible for the Western Church to become independent of secular monarchs and of the Eastern Emperor, when the Eastern Church did not achieve comparable independence?

How do legal and historical fictions (such as the Donation of Constantine, or Charlemagne's claim that the imperial throne was 'vacant') function to legitimize political power in a society that reveres antique authority?

Is 'the Dark Ages' a meaningful global category, or only a description of the temporary eclipse of Western Europe within a world where other civilizations (Tang China, the Islamic Caliphate) were flourishing?

philosophers_discussed.name: Lorenzo Valla
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Renaissance humanist (ca. 1406-57) mentioned as the first to expose the Donation of Constantine as a forgery (1439), on philological grounds -- its Latin could not be eighth-century usage claiming to be fourth-century; Russell notes the irony that he was later made apostolic secretary by Pope Nicholas V.

core_concepts.name: The mutual dependence of Pope and Emperor
core_concepts.plain_explanation: After Charlemagne's coronation in 800, no one could legitimately become Holy Roman Emperor without being crowned by the Pope in Rome, but for centuries every strong emperor also claimed the right to appoint or depose popes. Neither office could fully dominate the other, so the two were locked in a relationship of galling but, for centuries, unavoidable mutual need.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's account of the medieval theory of legitimate authority as resting jointly on Pope and Emperor: the Emperor derives legitimacy from papal coronation, while the Pope's temporal security and much of his authority historically depended on imperial protection and patronage.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This structural interdependence produced centuries of recurring conflict (culminating in the Investiture Controversy and the thirteenth-century struggles covered in later chapters), and its final breakdown in the fifteenth century -- through the rise of national monarchies and the Reformation -- ended the medieval unity of Christendom.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Begins with Charlemagne's coronation by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day, A.D. 800, itself made possible by Charlemagne's legal fiction that the imperial throne was vacant because the reigning Eastern sovereign, Irene, could not be Emperor as a woman.
examples: Charlemagne deriving his claim to legitimacy from the Pope while also protecting and effectively controlling the papacy
The later, more extreme conflict between Pope and Emperor culminating at Canossa (covered in Chapter IX)
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Sets up the entire Guelf-Ghibelline conflict and the investiture disputes treated in Chapters IX through XII.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: This is itself a claim about the fusion of religious and secular legitimacy in medieval political theory.

core_concepts.name: The Donation of Constantine
core_concepts.plain_explanation: A document forged by churchmen, probably around the time of Pepin's gift of Italian territory to the Pope, claiming that the Emperor Constantine had given Pope Sylvester and his successors dominion over Rome and the whole Western Empire when Constantine moved his capital East. It was believed genuine throughout the Middle Ages and used to justify the Pope's temporal power over the Papal States.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A forged imperial decree, accepted as authentic until Lorenzo Valla's philological exposure of it as a fabrication in 1439, that served as the legal-historical basis for papal claims to temporal sovereignty in Italy.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It gave 'an air of antique legality' to Pepin's eighth-century donation of Ravenna and the Exarchate, illustrating the medieval habit of legitimizing new arrangements through fabricated appeals to ancient authority.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Forged in connection with Pepin's donation to the papacy (754), to make the Pope's temporal possessions appear to derive from imperial grant rather than mere Frankish military conquest.
examples: C. Delisle Burns's summary of its fantastical narrative: Constantine's leprosy, his vision of Peter and Paul, his baptism by Sylvester, and his supposed grant of 'Rome and all the provinces...of Italy and the West' to the Roman Church
objections: Lorenzo Valla's 1439 philological demonstration that its Latin could not be genuine fourth-century usage
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Even after being exposed as a forgery, Pope Nicholas V (who made Valla his secretary) did not relinquish the States of the Church whose title had rested on it.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly underwrites the Church's claim to temporal, not merely spiritual, sovereignty in central Italy.

core_concepts.name: Russell's critique of 'the Dark Ages' as a Eurocentric label
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Russell argues that calling 600-1000 the 'Dark Ages' reflects an unwarranted concentration on Western Europe: during this same period China enjoyed the Tang dynasty's golden age of poetry, and Islamic civilization from Spain to India was brilliant and dominant in both power and culture. Western Europe's later global dominance was not foreordained and should not be read backward into this period.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's explicit argument that the loss suffered by Christendom in this period 'was not lost to civilization, but quite the contrary,' and that most of the cultural content of Western civilization itself derives from the Eastern Mediterranean (Greeks and Jews), not from any innate Western superiority.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It reframes the entire period covered by Part II: what looks like darkness from a narrowly Western viewpoint was, globally, an era of other civilizations' brilliance, and Western dominance from the Renaissance onward is treated by Russell as historically contingent rather than natural or permanent.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Prompted by Russell's survey of the low point of Western Christendom around the year 1000, contrasted with contemporaneous Tang China and the Islamic Caliphate.
examples: The Tang dynasty as 'the greatest age of Chinese poetry'
'the brilliant civilization of Islam' flourishing 'from India to Spain'
competing_positions: The conventional Eurocentric narrative that treats the whole world as passing through a 'Dark Age' in this period

core_concepts.name: Legal fiction as a medieval mode of legitimation
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Medieval rulers and institutions habitually justified new arrangements by claiming continuity with old, legitimate authority rather than admitting innovation -- for example, Charlemagne's argument that the imperial throne was legally 'vacant' (because a woman, Irene, could not be Emperor) rather than simply claiming it by conquest.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's observation that 'the Middle Ages were peculiarly addicted to legal fictions,' using the persistence of formally 'legitimate' claims (however fictional) to mask real shifts in power.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It explains how radical changes -- the effective end of Byzantine authority over the West, or the transfer of the imperial title to a Frankish king -- could be presented as continuous with, rather than a break from, established Roman legal order.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Illustrated by Charlemagne's coronation in 800 and, more broadly, by the medieval habit (which Russell revisits in Chapter XI) of parties justifying new institutions through antiquarian or archaistic argument.
examples: Charlemagne's claim that the throne of the Roman Empire was vacant because Irene, a woman, could not legitimately be Emperor
The Donation of Constantine as a legal fiction underpinning the Papal States
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes the same pattern recurs throughout the Middle Ages, for instance in the way twelfth-century parties in the empire-versus-papacy conflict all appealed to supposedly ancient precedent (Chapter XI).
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Fuses political legitimacy with religious sanction (coronation by the Pope).

arguments.title: Why the papacy, unlike the Eastern patriarchate, achieved independence from secular and imperial control
premises: The patriarch of Constantinople remained subject to the Emperor's authority over doctrine and appointments, and never achieved superiority over other Eastern patriarchs (Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem).

The Pope, by contrast, was the only patriarch in the West, combined the prestige of imperial Rome with the legends of Peter and Paul's martyrdom, and eventually broke free of Byzantine control after the Lombard capture of Ravenna (751) forced an alliance with the Franks instead.
In the West the laity remained largely illiterate for centuries, giving the clergy a relative advantage in influence that they lacked in the more literate East.
No Western monarch's prestige could match the Pope's, whereas the Eastern Emperor's prestige generally exceeded the patriarch's.
arguments.conclusion: These combined circumstances -- political accident (the Lombard conquest of Ravenna), historical prestige, and social conditions (Western illiteracy) -- rather than any doctrinal necessity, explain why the Western Church developed a papal monarchy while the Eastern Church did not.
arguments.explanation: Russell frames this as a matter of contingent historical circumstance, not an inevitable consequence of Christian doctrine, underscoring how much of subsequent Church history depended on these specific eighth-century events.
implications: Explains the structural conditions for everything that follows in Part II: papal supremacy in the West made possible the later conflicts with the Empire and the doctrinal authority the Church would later exercise over the scholastic philosophers.

arguments.title: Why the year 1000 marks the turning point of Western civilization
premises: Monastic reform (beginning with Cluny, though its main development belongs to the following chapter) began to revive moral and institutional discipline within the Church.

The waves of conquest by Mohammedans and by northern barbarians (Goths, Lombards, Hungarians, Normans) ceased around this time, at least as far as Western Europe was concerned, as the Normans -- the last vigorous conquerors -- were converted and settled.
arguments.conclusion: From approximately the year 1000, an upward movement in Western civilization began that, in Russell's judgment, continued until 1914.
arguments.explanation: Russell explicitly rejects the popular idea that a special dread of the world's end in the year 1000 marked the period; instead he treats the date as significant for these two concrete historical reasons.
implications: Frames the remaining chapters of Part II (monastic and papal reform, the eleventh-century revival of philosophy, the twelfth and thirteenth centuries) as chapters of ascent rather than decline.

key_distinctions: The Eastern Church's subordination to imperial authority vs. the Western Church's achievement of papal independence
Genuine Roman/imperial legitimacy vs. the 'usurper' status attributed to unrecognized barbarian kings
The narrowly Western sense of 'the Dark Ages' vs. the simultaneous flourishing of Tang China and the Islamic world
Legal fiction (continuity with antique authority) vs. the underlying reality of new political arrangements
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: The chapter follows directly from the account (in the preceding chapter) of Gregory the Great, Benedict, and Justinian, whose institutions (the papacy, monasticism, and Roman law) Russell says 'tamed the barbarians' despite the men themselves being culturally inferior to their predecessors.
connections_to_later_philosophers: The political framework established here -- an independent, increasingly powerful papacy in tension with a Holy-Roman-Imperial power dependent on papal coronation -- is the stage on which the eleventh-century revival of philosophy (Chapter IX), the investiture conflict, and the entire scholastic enterprise described through Chapter XIV will play out.
political_social_context: Covers the Lombard invasions of Italy, the Franco-papal alliance under Pepin and Charlemagne, the coronation of Charlemagne as Holy Roman Emperor (800), the reign of Nicholas I and his conflicts with Lothar II and the Patriarch Ignatius/Photius, the ninth- and tenth-century raids of Saracens, Magyars, and Normans, and the tenth-century domination of the papacy by the Roman aristocratic family of Theophylact and Marozia (the so-called 'pornocracy,' including Popes Sergius III, John XI, and John XII).
religion_science_culture_context: Discusses the Carolingian cultural revival under Alcuin (educated at York under Ecgbert, pupil of Bede's student), Saint Boniface's papally-directed conversion of Germany (as against Irish missionary influence), and the English monastic culture of Bede's Jarrow and Alcuin's York -- contrasted with the near-total collapse of learning during the ninth- and tenth-century invasions.
russell_presentation: Russell narrates this period largely as political and ecclesiastical history rather than philosophy, tracing the papacy's dependence on, then independence from, first Byzantium and then the Carolingian Empire, and its subsequent capture by the Roman aristocracy in the depraved 'pornocracy' of the tenth century. He is candid and unsentimental about the moral failings of the era's great men -- quoting at length a historian's account of Charlemagne's dissolute court and noting bluntly that Charlemagne 'saw to it that popes obeyed his orders.' His most emphatic authorial intervention comes at the chapter's close: he explicitly criticizes the Eurocentrism of the term 'Dark Ages,' insists that Western civilizational dominance since the Renaissance is a historical contingency rather than an inherent superiority, and -- writing during the Second World War -- expresses hope that the postwar world will 'admit Asia to equality in our thoughts, not only politically, but culturally.' This closing passage is Russell's own reflection, addressed to his contemporary readers, rather than historical reporting.
key_takeaways: The papacy's independence from Byzantium was secured largely by accident -- the Lombard capture of Ravenna (751) -- rather than by any inherent doctrinal necessity, and this independence, sealed by Pepin's donation and Charlemagne's coronation (800), created the papal-imperial structure that shaped medieval European politics.

The Donation of Constantine, a forgery used to legitimize the Pope's temporal power, was accepted as genuine throughout the Middle Ages and was not exposed until Lorenzo Valla's philological critique in 1439.
Charlemagne's coronation created a lasting, mutually dependent but often hostile relationship between Pope and Emperor that structured European politics for centuries.

The tenth century saw the papacy fall under the near-total control of the Roman aristocratic family of Theophylact and Marozia, marking the institutional low point before the eleventh-century reform movement.

Russell treats the year 1000 as a genuine historical turning point (due to monastic reform and the cessation of barbarian and Mohammedan invasions), not because of any special millennial dread, which he says did not in fact widely occur.

Russell explicitly challenges the Eurocentrism of 'the Dark Ages' as a label, pointing to the simultaneous flourishing of Tang China and the Islamic world, and treats Western global dominance as a contingent, possibly temporary, historical fact.
study_notes:
This chapter is best read as scene-setting rather than philosophy proper: nothing here is a philosophical argument in the sense the later chapters on Anselm, Aquinas, or Occam will offer. What it establishes is the institutional machinery -- an independent, increasingly centralized papacy locked in structural tension with a Holy Roman Empire that needed papal coronation to be legitimate -- inside of which medieval philosophy will later be produced, debated, and sometimes suppressed (as with John the Scot's book, condemned and ordered burned, discussed in the next chapter).

Pay particular attention to Russell's closing paragraphs, which are uncharacteristically present-tense and personal for a work otherwise written in the historian's past tense. Writing in the middle of the Second World War, Russell uses the 'Dark Ages' -- a period when Western Europe was genuinely eclipsed in both power and culture by Tang China and the Islamic Caliphate -- to make an argument about cultural relativism and the contingency of Western dominance that is really addressed to his own twentieth-century moment, not simply to the ninth or tenth centuries. This is a good example of Russell using history to make a live argument about his own present, and it is worth noting as an instance of authorial voice rather than neutral historical reporting.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A forged ancient document, believed genuine for centuries, in which the Emperor Constantine supposedly gave the Pope control over Rome and the whole Western Empire.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: An eighth-century forgery attributed to Constantine, used to provide antique legal justification for the papacy's temporal sovereignty over the Papal States; accepted as authentic throughout the medieval period and exposed as a fabrication by Lorenzo Valla in 1439.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The revived Western Roman Empire, founded when Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne Emperor on Christmas Day, 800, which lasted (in one form or another) until Napoleon's time.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The medieval and early-modern political entity founded by Charlemagne's imperial coronation, whose constitution assumed a theoretical harmony between Pope and Emperor, and whose relationship to the papacy was one of structural interdependence and recurring conflict.
related_concepts: The mutual dependence of Pope and Emperor

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A modern nickname for the period in the tenth century when the Roman noblewoman Marozia and her family effectively controlled the selection of popes, including her own son and grandson.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's account of the tenth-century domination of the papacy by the Theophylact-Marozia family of Roman aristocrats, exemplified by Popes Sergius III, John XI (Marozia's son), and John XII (her grandson, elected at sixteen), whose 'debauched life' Russell quotes the Cambridge Medieval History as describing.
related_concepts: Russell's critique of 'the Dark Ages' as a Eurocentric label

questions.prompt: What event forced the papacy into a permanent political break from the Eastern Empire, and what alliance replaced it?
questions.answer: The Lombard capture of Ravenna, the capital of Byzantine Italy, in about 751, exposed the popes to Lombard conquest while freeing them from Byzantine control; they responded by allying with the Franks, culminating in Pepin's donation of Ravenna and the former Exarchate to the papacy in 754.
questions.explanation: This alliance created the Papal States and set the stage for Charlemagne's later coronation as Emperor.

questions.prompt: What was the Donation of Constantine, and who first exposed it as a forgery?
questions.answer: A forged decree purporting to record Constantine's grant of Rome and the Western Empire to Pope Sylvester and his successors; it was used to legitimize the Pope's temporal power. It was first exposed as a forgery by the Renaissance humanist Lorenzo Valla in 1439, on the philological grounds that its Latin was not authentic fourth-century usage.
questions.explanation: Russell notes the irony that Valla was afterward made apostolic secretary by Pope Nicholas V, who nonetheless retained the Papal States.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, why is calling the period 600-1000 the 'Dark Ages' a narrowly Western judgment?
questions.answer: Because during this same period China experienced the Tang dynasty, its greatest age of poetry, and the Islamic world from India to Spain enjoyed a brilliant civilization; what Western Christendom lost in this period was not lost to civilization generally, and Western global dominance did not become established until much later.
questions.explanation: Russell uses this point to argue that Western Europe's later cultural and political dominance was a historical contingency, not a natural or permanent state of affairs.

questions.prompt: Which Renaissance humanist first demonstrated, on grounds of Latin style, that the Donation of Constantine was a forgery?
questions.explanation: Valla's philological method -- showing that the document's Latin could not be genuine fourth-century usage -- is an early landmark of critical historical scholarship.

questions.prompt: What legal fiction did Charlemagne use to justify his claim to the imperial throne, and why?
questions.answer: He maintained that the imperial throne was vacant because the reigning Eastern sovereign, Irene, who called herself emperor rather than empress, was a usurper, since (in this view) no woman could legitimately be emperor.
questions.explanation: This illustrates the medieval habit of legitimizing innovation through claims of continuity with prior legitimate authority.

questions.prompt: Contrast the position of the patriarch of Constantinople with that of the Pope of Rome in relation to secular imperial power.
questions.answer: The patriarch of Constantinople remained subject to the Emperor, who claimed authority to decide matters of faith and to appoint or depose bishops and patriarchs; he also had to share prestige with other Eastern patriarchs (Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem). The Pope, by contrast, was the sole Western patriarch, eventually broke free of Byzantine control after the loss of Ravenna, and became the sole source of imperial legitimacy in the West through the coronation of emperors.
questions.explanation: This contrast explains why the Western Church developed a centralized papal monarchy while the Eastern Church did not, and it underlies the eventual schism between the Eastern and Western Churches.

questions.prompt: What two developments does Russell credit with making the year 1000 a genuine historical turning point for Western Europe?
questions.answer: First, the beginning of monastic reform, which gradually revived moral and institutional discipline in the Church. Second, the cessation of conquest by both Mohammedans and northern barbarians in Western Europe, as the last wave of conquerors (the Normans) settled and converted to Christianity.
questions.explanation: Russell explicitly rejects the popular belief that a special dread of the world's end in the year 1000 was widespread, treating this instead as a matter of concrete historical circumstance.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's argument for why the Western Church achieved independence from secular and imperial authority, while the Eastern Church did not.
questions.answer: Premise: the patriarch of Constantinople remained doctrinally and administratively subordinate to the Emperor and shared prestige with other Eastern patriarchs. Premise: the Pope was the sole Western patriarch, combined imperial Rome's prestige with the legends of Peter and Paul's martyrdom, and (through the accident of the Lombard capture of Ravenna) was forced into an alliance with the Franks rather than remaining dependent on Byzantium. Premise: Western lay illiteracy gave the clergy comparatively greater social influence than in the more literate East. Conclusion: these contingent circumstances, not any doctrinal necessity, explain the papacy's rise to independent, monarchical authority in the West.
questions.explanation: This argument frames the entire structural backdrop against which the rest of Part II's history of medieval philosophy unfolds.
